title: In his image (CCC 356–357)
hookLine: every human being is someone, not something

lines: THE DELIVERY. THE NEW HIRE. THE GUY IN 4B.
cards: Listen to how people talk on an ordinary day. The delivery. The new hire.
The guy in 4B. My ride is two minutes away. The customer on line three.
None of it is cruel; it's just fast. A person becomes the job they're doing, and everyone moves on. The first chapter of the Bible says the opposite.
It puts an invisible mark on every one of those people: made on purpose, to the image of God. The Catechism's short phrase: a person is someone, not something.

teach.h: TO THE IMAGE OF GOD HE CREATED HIM.
teach.b: Start with the text. On the sixth day, in the Douay-Rheims, God says: "Let us make man to our image and likeness."
Then: "And God created man to his own image: to the image of God he created him. Male and female he created them." In Latin, image of God is imago Dei, today's word. Second, what an image was.
In the ancient world, some scholars point out, kings set up statues of themselves in the lands they ruled: I'm present here, this belongs to me.

teach.h: A KING'S STATUE, GIVEN TO EVERYONE.
teach.b: Genesis hands that royal idea to everyone: the farmer, the servant, the child. Every human being is God's image set down in the world. Third, the Catechism.
The human person, it teaches, is the only creature on earth God willed for its own sake, able to know oneself, to give oneself freely, and to enter into friendship with God.
That's why the Church says a person has dignity: not a thing to be used, but someone. Some early Christian writers, like Irenaeus, told image and likeness apart.
The image, they said, is never lost; the likeness, a life that actually resembles God, can be damaged and restored. Fourth, the hard part.

teach.h: IN EVERYONE, OR IT MEANS NOTHING.
teach.b: The image is in everyone or it means nothing.
The person you admire, yes. And the person who cut you off in traffic, the prisoner, the stranger whose language you don't speak, the baby, the dying.
Catholics ground their social teaching right here, in this one verse about who people are.

how: Catholics learn in catechism that every person is made in the image of God, and the Church's social teaching on the poor, the unborn, the sick, migrants and prisoners is built on that dignity.

the soul's return to God at death

s: in Genesis, only kings bear God's image
Genesis gives the royal idea of an image to every human being, male and female.
the Catechism calls the human the only creature on earth God willed for its own sake
it teaches that each person is willed for their own sake, able to know, give and love.
for Irenaeus, the image of God can be completely lost
he told them apart: the image remains; the likeness can be damaged and restored.

games.q: in the ancient world, a king set up statues of himself to show who ruled a land. how does Genesis use the idea of an image?
o: it gives the image only to the priests.
it gives the image to every human being.
it forbids the idea of an image entirely.
games.why: every human, male and female, is made to the image of God. a royal idea becomes everyone's dignity.

practice: Bring to mind one face you saw today, maybe someone you barely noticed, a cashier, a driver, a coworker, and say quietly: someone, not something.
Then, if you can, hold a harder face, someone who annoys you; you don't have to feel warm, just let them be a person for a minute. If you pray, you can offer each face to God.

wordCard.voice: Imago Dei. Latin for the image of God: what Genesis says every human being is made in, and why the Church says each person has a dignity no one can take away. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: in the image of God. Latin renders it imago Dei.

carryVoice: Your line: someone, not something. From Aquinas to charity, the Trinity, creation, evil, angels, and now the human person: that was the week. See you tomorrow.
